faq.q: What is the hallmark imaging finding in PAP?

faq.a: Steroids are ineffective; lavage removes surfactant directly.
faq.q: Why is whole‑lung lavage preferred over steroids?

faq.a: Yes, especially in autoimmune cases; repeat lavage or GM‑CSF therapy may be needed.

exam: A 35‑year‑old man presents with progressive dyspnea and dry cough. HRCT shows crazy‑paving. What is the next diagnostic step? — BAL to confirm milky fluid and PAS positivity.
A patient with PAP develops haemoptysis. What immediate action should be taken? — Stabilise airway, give oxygen, consider bronchoscopy to localise bleed.
Why is whole‑lung lavage contraindicated in patients with severe pulmonary hypertension? — Risk of circulatory collapse during lavage.
A patient with known PAP is on GM‑CSF therapy but develops a fever. What is the likely complication? — Secondary infection due to immunosuppression.
What distinguishes PAP from pulmonary oedema on imaging? — PAP shows crazy‑paving with clear BAL; oedema shows alveolar infiltrates with clear BAL.
Why are steroids avoided in idiopathic PAP? — They do not reduce surfactant accumulation and may worsen infection risk.
ai.title: Pulmonary Alveolar Proteinosis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A rare interstitial lung disease where surfactant accumulates in alveoli, causing progressive dyspnea and hypoxia. Diagnosis relies on imaging, bronchoalveolar lavage, and GM-CSF autoantibody testing. Treatment centres on whole‑lung lavage and GM‑CSF therapy.

sections.p: Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP) is characterised by surfactant build‑up in alveoli, leading to impaired gas exchange. Diagnosis requires a combination of clinical suspicion, imaging, and confirmatory tests.

t.b: Ground‑glass opacities with a crazy‑paving pattern
Milky fluid with periodic acid‑Schiff‑positive lipoproteinaceous material
Positive in ~90% of idiopathic PAP, confirming autoimmune etiology

sections.p: Severity is graded by oxygen requirement and radiographic extent. The modified PFT score uses DLCO and PaO₂ to stage disease.

b: Genetic PAP: mutations in CSF2RA or CSF2RB
sections.p: Idiopathic autoimmune PAP is the commonest form. Other causes include secondary PAP from infections, inhalational exposures, and genetic defects.
Patients report progressive exertional dyspnea, dry cough, and occasionally weight loss. Physical exam may show crackles and clubbing.
Investigation strategy prioritises tests available locally and those that can be sent to reference labs.

t.b: Low DLCO indicates impaired gas transfer

sections.p: Rapid deterioration, haemoptysis, and superimposed infections are ominous. Secondary infections can be fatal.
First treat the underlying cause if secondary. Idiopathic PAP is managed with whole‑lung lavage; GM‑CSF therapy is reserved for refractory cases.

t.b: Physically removes accumulated surfactant, restoring ventilation
Recurrent or refractory PAP after lavage

b: Treat TB, HIV, and other infections aggressively
sections.p: Regular clinical review, PFTs, and imaging are essential. Preventive measures focus on avoiding inhalational exposures and treating infections promptly.
Differential includes diffuse interstitial lung diseases, pulmonary oedema, and pulmonary alveolar haemorrhage.

b: Early autoimmune PAP may have negative antibodies
sections.p: BAL may appear clear if lavage is inadequate; HRCT findings can mimic other ILDs; low GM‑CSF antibody titres may occur in early disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypoxia (PaO₂ <50 mmHg), haemoptysis, sudden worsening of dyspnea, or signs of infection
